source_text: πάλιν καὶ ἀνέθαλψε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἄνευ πραγματείας καὶ οἷον αὐτομάτως, ἅτε συνδημιουργὸς καὶ ἰσουργὸς τοῦ ὑποστήσαντος αὐτὴν κατ' ἀρχὰς ἀρχιτέχνου θεοῦ, ὡς γνῶναι ἡμῖν ἐφίεται, ἐξ ὧν ἐξέφηναν οὗτοι· Ἰώβ· «πνεῦμα θεῖον τὸ ποιῆσάν με· πνοὴ δὲ παντοκράτορος, ἡ διδάσκουσά με.» ∆αυὶδ ἐν μὲν ργʹ ψαλμῷ· «ἐξαποστελεῖς τὸ πνεῦμα σου καὶ κτισθήσονται, καὶ ἀνακαινιεῖς τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς.» τοῦτο βεβαιοῖ ὁ ἀπόστολος γράφων Κορινθίοις τὸ δεύτερον· «ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις· τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, ἰδοὺ γέγονε καινὰ τὰ πάντα.» ἐν δὲ λβʹ ψαλμῷ· «τῷ λόγῳ κυρίου οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν, καὶ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στό ματος αὐτοῦ πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις αὐτῶν» μὴ παραδράμῃς τὰ αὐτόθεν ἀκούεσθαι δυνάμενα· ἀλλ' ἴδε, ὅτιπερ–ὡς δημιουργὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς θεός–μένον εἰς ἀεὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ φιλίαν μόνιμον τῇ κτίσει χορηγεῖ καὶ ἀλύτοις αὐτὴν ἔσφιγξε δεσμοῖς καὶ ἥδρασεν. ἀκατάσειστον καὶ πάντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ δυνάμει στηρίζει· καὶ ὅτι ἀθέμιτόν ἐστι κτίσμα καλεῖν τὸ κτίζον καὶ ἐνδυναμοῦν τοῦ θεοῦ τὰ κτίσματα. συνεργὸν γὰρ καὶ 69 ὁμοούσιον αὐτὸ τῷ θεῷ ἅτε πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ καὶ δάκτυλον, ὡς ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ ἐδείχθη βιβλίῳ, μυστικῶς παριστῶν ἐν ηʹ ψαλμῷ προφητεύει· «ὅτι ὄψομαι τοὺς οὐρανούς, ἔργα τῶν δακτύλων σου.» καὶ Μωυσῆς δὲ ἐν τῇ γενέσει ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς πρὸς τὸν υἱὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον αὐτοῦ πνεῦμα φησίν· «ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν καὶ ἀρχέτω σαν τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.» οὐ γὰρ ἀγγέλους ἢ ἄλλα πνεύματα ἔλαβεν συγχειρουργοὺς ἢ γνωμοδότας ὁ θεός· «ἐπειδὴ ὁ δοῦλος οὐκ οἶδεν, τί ποιεῖ αὐτοῦ ὁ δεσπότης.» οὐδὲ εὑρίσκεται πώποτε εἰς δημιουργίαν συμπαραλαβὼν κτίσμα, καθὰ ∆αυὶδ ψάλλει ἐν λβʹ ψαλμῷ· «ὁ πλάσας καταμονὰς τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν,» καὶ ἐν ρληʹ· «οὐκ ἐκρύβη τὸ ὀστοῦν μου ἀπὸ σοῦ, ὃ ποίησας ἐν κρυφῇ.» καὶ ὡς Παῦλος Ῥωμαίοις γράφει· «τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου; ἢ τίς σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο;» τουτέστιν, τῆς κτίσεως οὐδείς. πλάτος γὰρ ἔχον τὸ «τίς» τοῦτο προφαίνει. ἔδειξεν δὲ τῷ μὲν μὴ εἰπεῖν «ποιήσατε», ἀλλὰ «ποιήσωμεν», ὡς οὐκ ἔστιν ὑπουργὸς ὁ υἱὸς καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ἀλλὰ δυνάμεως καὶ θελήσεως μιᾶς· τῷ δὲ ἐπαγαγεῖν «κατ' εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν», ὡς μία ἐστὶν οὐσία τῇ τριάδι· καὶ ὡς οὐ πρὸς ἀγγέλους εἴρηται τοῦτο τοῖς ἀπείρως καὶ ἀσυνεικάστως ἔν μείω τὴν «εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν» ἔχουσιν εἰ ἀκίνδυνον τοῦτο, ὡς ἄνθρωπον, εἰπεῖν τῆς ἀνειδέου καὶ ἀσχηματίστου καὶ ἀρρήτου τριάδος, διὸ ἐπήγαγεν ὁ αὐτὸς κοσμογράφος· «καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον· κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν· ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς· καὶ εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς·» καὶ πάλιν· «εἶδεν ὁ θεός, ὅτι καλόν.» ἐν οἷς ῥητοῖς αὖθις τῆς αὐτοτελοῦς καὶ γενεσιουργοῦ τριάδος τὸ τέλειον καὶ σύμφωνον καὶ κοσμητικὸν καὶ ἐπίπαν ἄφθονον σημαίνεται μυστικῶς. ἐπειδὴ ταῦτα θεάτρων μὲν καὶ πλήθους ἄξια οὐχ ἡγήσατο εἶναι ὁ Μωυσῆς ἤγουν ὁ ἐνηχήσας αὐτῷ θεός· τοσούτων δέ, ὅσοι μὴ παρανομεῖν ἐς ταῦτα ἔμελλον. «ἐποίησεν» γὰρ «ὁ θεός», τουτέστιν ὁ υἱός, «τὸν ἄνθρωπον κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ», τουτέστιν τοῦ πατρός, «ἐποίησεν αὐτόν, καὶ εἶδεν ὁ θεός», τουτέστιν τὸ πνεῦμα «ὅτι καλόν, καὶ εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς», τουτέστιν ἡγίασεν. τὸ δὲ «κατ' εἰκόνα», ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, νοητέον, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ θεϊκοῦ φυσήματος τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἀθάνατον ἔχομεν καὶ νοῦν ἀεὶ θέοντα καὶ κυβερνῶντα ἐφ' ὃ χρή, καὶ λόγον σοφὸν ἀρέσκοντα τῷ δεδωκότι καὶ δυνάμενον σὺν πίστει τεκνογονίας αἴτιον γίνεσθαι καὶ ζωῆς καὶ νεκρῶν ἐγέρσεως καὶ ὀρέων μεταθέσεως· πρὸς τούτοις, ὅτι μετειλήφαμεν καὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀγαθότητος. εἶτα καὶ Παῦλος, ὡς μικρῷ πρόσθεν ἐλέχθη· «ζωοποιήσει καὶ τὰ θνητὰ ἡμῶν σώματα, διὰ τοῦ ἐνοικοῦντος αὐτοῦ πνεύματος ἐν ἡμῖν.» καὶ Ἑβραίοις τοὺς αἰῶνας γεγενῆσθαι καὶ τὴν κτίσιν ἐστηρίχθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος καταγγέλλων καὶ ῥῆμα θεοῦ τὸ πνεῦμα, καθὰ ἤδη ἐμνημονεύθη, προσαγορεύων γράφει· «πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι θεοῦ, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὸ βλεπόμενον γεγονέναι,» καὶ πάλιν· «φέρων γὰρ τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ,» καὶ ὁ ψαλμῳδός· «πάντα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐποίησας,» τουτέστιν ἐν τῷ πνεύματί σου καὶ τῷ υἱῷ σου. πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἄναρχον καὶ δημιουργὸν καὶ κυρίως θεὸς τὸ θεϊκὸν πνεῦμα τὸ ἀχώριστον τοῦ πνεύσαντος αὐτὸ καὶ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ υἱοῦ· τὸ τοὺς αἰῶνας κατασκευάσαν, μεθ' ὧν οὐρανός τε καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ πᾶν, εἴ τί ἐστιν κτιστὸν παρήχθη· καὶ πάντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ δυνάμει φέρον τε καὶ διοικοῦν· τὸ παραυτίκα τοῦ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... and the earth, having been swept down together with human lawless deeds, he renewed] again and warmed back to life — the Holy Spirit — without labour and as it were of itself, inasmuch as fellow-creator and equal-worker of the master-craftsman God who gave it [the earth] subsistence in the beginning, as it is permitted to us to know, from the things which these declared: Job: 'a divine Spirit, the one having made me; and breath of the Almighty, the one teaching me.' David in the 103rd psalm (LXX; English 104): 'you will send out your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.' This the apostle confirms, writing to the Corinthians the second [time]: 'so that if anyone [is] in Christ, [he is] a new creation; the old things passed by, behold all things have become new.' And in the 32nd psalm (LXX; English 33): 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth [the word split across a line] all their powers.' Do not run past the things able to be heard straight from there; but see that — as creator and good God — the Spirit of God, remaining for ever, supplies to the creation a lasting friendship and bound it tight with unloosable bonds and set it firm. Unshakable, it also supports all things by its own power; and that it is unlawful to call creature the one creating and strengthening the creatures of God. For presenting it mystically as fellow-worker and [page number 69, debris] of one essence with God, inasmuch as his Spirit and finger, as was shown in the first book, he prophesies in the 8th psalm: 'for I will see the heavens, works of your fingers.' And Moses too in Genesis, from God and Father to the Son and his Holy Spirit, says: 'let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let them rule [the word split across a line] over the things on the earth.' For God did not take angels or other spirits as fellow-handworkers or counsel-givers: 'since the slave does not know what his master does.' Nor is he ever found having taken along a creature for creation, as David sings in the 32nd psalm (LXX; English 33): 'the one having fashioned their hearts alone,' and in the 138th (LXX; English 139): 'my bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.' And as Paul writes to the Romans: 'for who knew the mind of the Lord? Or who became his counsellor?' that is, of the creation no one. For the 'who', having breadth, shows this forth. And he showed, by not saying 'make [plural]' but 'let us make', that the Son and the Holy Spirit is not an underling but of one power and will; and by adding 'according to our image and likeness', that there is one essence for the Trinity; and that this has not been said to angels, who have 'the image and likeness' infinitely and incomparably in a lesser [degree], if it is without danger to say this, as a man, of the formless and shapeless and unspeakable Trinity; wherefore the same world-writer added: 'and God made man; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them; and he blessed them'; and again: 'God saw that [it was] good.' In which sayings again the perfect and harmonious and adorning and altogether unstinting [character] of the self-complete and becoming-working Trinity is signified mystically. Since Moses, or rather the God who sounded [it] into him, did not consider these things worthy of theatres and of a crowd, but of as many as were not going to act lawlessly toward these things. For 'God', that is the Son, 'made man according to the image of God', that is of the Father, 'he made him, and God saw', that is the Spirit, 'that [it was] good, and he blessed them', that is, he sanctified. And the 'according to the image', as it seems to me, is to be understood: that from the divine breathing we have the immortal spirit, and a mind always running and steering toward what is needed, and wise speech pleasing to the one who has given [it], and able with faith to become cause of child-bearing and of life and of raising of the dead and of moving of mountains; in addition to these, that we have also received a share of his goodness. Then also Paul, as was said a little before: 'he will give life also to our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us.' And to the Hebrews, proclaiming that the ages came to be and the creation was made firm by the Holy Spirit, and addressing the Spirit as word of God, as was already mentioned, he writes: 'by faith we understand the ages to have been framed by a word of God, so that what is seen has not come to be from things appearing'; and again: 'for bearing all things by the word of his power'; and the psalmist: 'you made all things in wisdom', that is, in your Spirit and your Son. How then [is] the divine Spirit not beginningless and creator and properly God, the one inseparable from the one who breathed it and from the creator Son; the one having built the ages, with which both heaven and the things in it and everything, if anything is created, was brought forth; and the one bearing and governing all things by its own power; the one at the very moment of the [continues in the next section: ... coming into being of heaven, earth, sea, being borne upon the water] ...
pass_b_english: …again and warmed it back to life: the Holy Spirit did, without toil and as if of his own accord, being fellow-creator and equal in working with God, the master craftsman who gave the earth its being in the beginning. So we are permitted to know from what these have declared. Job: “A divine Spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me” (Job 33:4). David, in the hundred and fourth Psalm: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:30). The apostle confirms this, writing to the Corinthians the second time: “So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). And in the thirty-third Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6).

Do not run past what can be heard straight from these words. See rather that the Spirit of God, as creator and good God, abiding for ever, supplies the creation with a lasting friendship, has bound it fast with bonds that cannot be loosed, and has set it firm. Unshaken, he also upholds all things by his own power. See too that it is unlawful to call a creature him who creates and gives strength to the creatures of God. For the psalmist, presenting him in a hidden way as God’s fellow-worker and of one essence with God, since he is his Spirit and his finger, as was shown in the first book, prophesies in the eighth Psalm: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8:3).

Moses too, in Genesis, speaking for God the Father to the Son and to his Holy Spirit, says: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let them rule over the things on the earth” (Genesis 1:26). For God did not take angels or other spirits as fellow-workers or advisers, “since the servant does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15). Nor is he ever found to have taken a creature along with him for the work of creation, as David sings in the thirty-third Psalm: “He who fashioned their hearts by himself alone” (Psalm 33:15); and in the hundred and thirty-ninth: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Psalm 139:15). And as Paul writes to the Romans: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Romans 11:34); that is, no one in creation. For the word “who,” being broad, makes this plain.

By not saying “Make” but “Let us make,” he showed that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not underlings, but of one power and one will; and by adding “according to our image and likeness,” that the Trinity has one essence. He showed too that this was not said to angels, who have “the image and likeness” in a measure infinitely and incomparably less, if it is safe for one who is only a man to say this of the Trinity, which has no form, no shape, and is beyond speech. Therefore the same writer of the world’s making added: “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them, and he blessed them” (Genesis 1:27-28); and again: “God saw that it was good.” In these words, once more, the perfection, harmony, ordering beauty and all-embracing bounty of the self-complete Trinity, author of all that comes to be, are signified in a hidden way. For Moses, or rather God who sounded these words in his ears, did not think them fit for theatres and the crowd, but only for as many as would not sin against them. For “God made” (that is, the Son) “man according to the image of God” (that is, of the Father), “he made him; and God saw” (that is, the Spirit) “that it was good, and he blessed them,” that is, he sanctified them.

“According to the image,” as it seems to me, should be understood in this way: that from the divine breathing we have the immortal spirit, and a mind ever in motion and steering toward what it ought, and wise speech, pleasing to the one who gave it, which with faith can become the cause of the begetting of children, of life, of the raising of the dead and of the moving of mountains; and besides these, that we have also received a share in his goodness.

Then Paul too, as was said a little before: “He will give life also to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us” (Romans 8:11). And to the Hebrews, proclaiming that the ages came into being and the creation was made firm by the Holy Spirit, and calling the Spirit the word of God, as has already been mentioned, he writes: “By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that appear” (Hebrews 11:3); and again: “For he upholds all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). And the psalmist: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 104:24), that is, in your Spirit and in your Son. How, then, is the divine Spirit not without beginning, and creator, and God in the proper sense? He is inseparable from him who breathed him forth and from the creator Son; he built the ages, and with them were brought forth heaven, what is in it, and everything else that is created; he bears and governs all things by his own power; he, at the very moment of the …

choices.issue: Garbled draft, wrong Psalm numbers, abbreviated references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u17): retranslated. The old English printed wrong Psalm numbers in the reading text: 'Psalm 33' for ργʹ (English 104), 'Psalm 77' for λβʹ (English 33) twice, 'Psalm 84' for ηʹ (8) and 'Psalm 50' for ρληʹ (English 139). It read ἀνέθαλψε as 'shone forth', made the Spirit the one God 'established' (αὐτὴν is the earth), and garbled μὴ παραδράμῃς ('Do not let it pass by that these can be heard from the original sources'), ἐνδυναμοῦν ('strengtheners'), καταμόνας ('dwellings'), the 'Let us make' argument ('he showed to the one [God] not to say make'), τοῖς ... ἐν μείω ... ἔχουσιν ('those who are unlearned'), ἐνηχήσας ('God had thundered to him'), θέοντα ('thinking'), προσαγορεύων ('approaching the subject') and μεθ' ὧν ('through whom'). It broke a sentence across paragraphs ('one essence in the...'). References: (2 Cor 5:17), (Gen 1:26), (Rom 11:34) written in full; (Genesis 1:26-28) -> (Genesis 1:27-28); (Genesis 1:31) dropped from the inline text and listed as possible. Brackets '[God]', '[things]' removed.

choices.term: πάλιν καὶ ἀνέθαλψε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον
choices.english: …again and warmed it back to life: the Holy Spirit did
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; the previous section ends 'the earth ... he renewed …'. τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον is the subject of the whole sentence begun there; 'did' names it without repeating the previous section's words.

choices.term: τοῦ ὑποστήσαντος αὐτὴν κατ' ἀρχὰς ἀρχιτέχνου θεοῦ
choices.english: God, the master craftsman who gave the earth its being in the beginning
choices.why: αὐτὴν is feminine and picks up τὴν γῆν; 'the earth' is written out because 'it' would be read as the Spirit.

choices.english: “A divine Spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me”
choices.why: Didymus quotes the Greek Job ('teaches me'); the Hebrew-based English has 'hath given me life'. Same verse, so the plain reference is kept.

choices.term: ἐν ργʹ / λβʹ / ηʹ / ρληʹ ψαλμῷ
choices.english: the hundred and fourth / thirty-third / eighth / hundred and thirty-ninth Psalm
choices.why: Greek Psalm numbers converted to English numbering (103 -> 104, 32 -> 33, 8 -> 8, 138 -> 139) and checked by verse text.

choices.english: has set it firm. Unshaken, he also upholds all things
choices.why: Follows the printed punctuation, taking ἀκατάσειστον with the Spirit; see problems.

choices.english: the psalmist, presenting him in a hidden way ..., prophesies in the eighth Psalm
choices.why: The verb has no expressed subject; the quotation is from the eighth Psalm, so 'the psalmist' is plain English, not a bracketed supplement.
Didymus' title for the Spirit (Luke 11:20 with Matthew 12:28), argued in his first book.
John 15:15; 'servant' as in the familiar wording.

choices.term: ὁ πλάσας καταμονὰς τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν
choices.english: He who fashioned their hearts by himself alone
choices.why: Didymus reads κατὰ μόνας as 'alone', proving that God took no creature as helper; the old 'dwellings' was wrong.
'Who' covers every creature, hence 'no one in creation'.
Read as ἐν μείω (μείων, less); the copy-text accent on ἔν is a print slip.

choices.english: for one who is only a man
choices.why: Didymus' hedge about speaking of the Trinity's image.

choices.english: the same writer of the world’s making
choices.why: Moses as author of the creation account.

choices.term: τὸ τέλειον καὶ σύμφωνον καὶ κοσμητικὸν καὶ ἐπίπαν ἄφθονον
choices.english: the perfection, harmony, ordering beauty and all-embracing bounty
choices.why: Neuter adjectives used as abstract nouns.
λόγος beside νοῦς is the gift of rational speech; it 'with faith' moves mountains, so 'speech' rather than 'reason'.

choices.english: calling the Spirit the word of God
choices.why: προσαγορεύω is 'call, name'; Didymus reads ῥῆμα in Hebrews 11:3 and 1:3 as the Spirit.

choices.term: πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἄναρχον ... τὸ παραυτίκα τοῦ
choices.english: How, then, is the divine Spirit not ...? He is inseparable ...; he, at the very moment of the …
choices.why: The question's appositive clauses are set as statements for readability; the last runs into the next section (γενέσθαι οὐρανόν ...), so only the words held here are translated, ending with '…'.
στό ματος and ἀρχέτω σαν are words split across printed lines; 69 is a printed page number, skipped.
